    #77723. Breaking: John Madden Deserved Better Than a Messy Amazon Biopic

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (927 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: John Madden Deserved Better Than a Messy Amazon Biopic

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, as a movie critic, I’m not in the business of telling professional filmmakers what they could or should do with their art.
    • In a recent development, streaming now on Prime Video, right on time for Thanksgiving football, is David O.
    • Devoid of suspense, stakes, or really any answer to the question “Why?” MADDEN is a plotless dud that falls short in its game blueprint of probing the unbearable weight of a massive legacy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, as a movie critic, I’m not in the business of telling professional filmmakers what they could or should do with their art. What an unproductive way to do my job. But sometimes I see something so egregious, and so boneheaded, I’m compelled to scream from my seat, forehead running hot and veins bulging out—like a coach forced to watch his wide receiver telegraph his route to the defense like a GPS in cleats. That’s how I felt watching MADDEN.

    In a recent development, streaming now on Prime Video, right on time for Thanksgiving football, is David O. Russell’s MADDEN. It’s a significant streaming snooze where Nicolas Cage dons a fat suit and putzes around in a confused performance that flip-flops on which part of the legendary coach-turned-broadcaster-turned-foot-spray-spokesman’s interiority we’re meant to sympathize with. The real John Madden suffered cognitive decline until his death in 2021, but Cage’s performance is another exhausting exercise of actors playing undiagnosed dementia—and MADDEN has no calcium in its bones to even commit to that.

    Devoid of suspense, stakes, or really any answer to the question “Why?” MADDEN is a plotless dud that falls short in its game blueprint of probing the unbearable weight of a massive legacy. Worst of all, the spine of a fantastic movie is all there. It’s just not in playing shape. To wit: Scrubbed from the trailers is the reason anyone under the age of 35 knows John Madden’s name: video games. (It is my personal conspiracy theory this was done to mitigate losing an audience of boomer granddads, who will fire up the movie on their Roku before passing out on tryptophan.) In 1988, the former Raiders coach who scribbled on screens lent his name to a project by a small tech company called Electronic Arts. Today it’s valued at $55 billion and owned by Saudis. But back then it was just a start-up full of nerds making a football-simulation video game called Madden NFL, which has since morphed into an industry juggernaut that rakes in the equivalent of a small country’s gross domestic product.

    Sources indicate that the men and women of Madden’s era are obviously unable to fathom computer games as a big deal. (Even now, on the eve of Grand Theft Auto VI, I have heard from people grossly underestimating its economic and cultural power.) In the film is John Mulaney as Trip Hawkins, the founder of EA, whose wiry physique, skinny ties, and plaid button-downs stand in contrast to the movie’s many beefcake extras who exude ’70s-flavored machismo. But Trip’s presence in the film exists to warn the chain-smoking dinosaurs of their coming extinction. Cementing a legacy is not about winning so much that they make a bronze bust and stick you in the Hall of Fame, with the other dead guys. It’s about making your name mean something. No one sees the future until it’s in front of them—you can only hope you can find your way to be part of it somehow. And somehow John Madden did just that. Unfortunately, even MADDEN fails to recognize the awesome potential of its own story.

    Industry observers note that russell’s latest work spends the first half cosplaying as a sober sports biopic, in the vein of Moneyball, until it eventually and perhaps inevitably pivots into a low-stakes tech-business success story like BlackBerry or AIR. This alone isn’t a bad thing—frankly, it should be the entire movie—but MADDEN’s failure to synthesize its core themes about how men can actually live forever is what makes the movie such a frustrating experience to sit through.

    In a recent development, MADDEN (the movie, all caps) is concerned with legacy. What does it mean? What does it really take to be remembered? For Cage’s Madden, it starts out as a straightforward idea: win Super Bowls. Football runs in his blood and runs his house; early on, Kathryn Hahn, as Madden’s wife, Virginia, scolds her son for rooting for the wrong team. Raiders football is what feeds and clothes them, she indicates. Thanking Raiders football is akin to thanking God. When the Raiders start winning and a retired Madden watches quite pathetically with a microphone in his hand, you can see the thousand-yard stare in his eyes as he considers abandoning his faith. Later, Christian Bale’s gel-slicked Al Davis, the owner of the Raiders whose rings form a set of brass knuckles, tries to convince Madden to come back—because winning is all it takes to be remembered, and winning is all that matters.

    Before this movie, I had never heard of Al Davis, but I have played plenty of Madden on PlayStation. By the end of the movie (minor spoilers), Cage spends Thanksgiving with his preteen granddaughter, who whomps his butt with a controller in her hands. You can see what MADDEN is getting at here. Real legacy cannot be measured in rings or bronze statues but in the joy you inspire in others. Like it or not, a best-selling video game is how today’s generation of professional athletes stayed interested in the sport, and it might be John Madden’s single greatest contribution to football, more than anything he’s ever done on the field.

    Sources indicate that unfortunately, Russell’s slipshod direction ensures that nothing in the movie clicks and nothing in it breathes. Trite dialogue and a flat visual palette that’s barely a notch above Hallmark movies keep it on the bench. As it stands, MADDEN is simply not the movie I would have made. But I’m just screaming from the nosebleeds.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that as a certified holistic health coach and wellness content creator, Carolina Salazar knows the importance of a peaceful wind-down routine before bed. She trusts Hubspace from The Home Depot that powers many of the smart devices in her home, to help ease her into a good night’s sleep.

    Hubspace, The Home Depot’s exclusive smart home platform, powers more than 250 products across select private brands—like Hampton Bay, Husky, and Vissani—as well as national brand partners. It effortlessly connects everyday essentials, including smart security, indoor and outdoor lighting, appliances, switches, watering controls, and more.

    Some of the Hubspace app’s most practical features help users personalize lighting and improve home security. Hubspace Connect, for example, lets you control compatible lighting from a single switch, while Vacation Mode is a security feature that turns lights and smart plugs on and off while you’re away. One of Salazar’s favorite features is Circadian Rhythm, which automatically transitions lights from cooler, whiter tones to warmer ones as the day goes on.

    Industry observers note that “I can set my lights to follow my circadian rhythm, so they shift automatically throughout the day,” says Salazar. “And when they start to turn warm in the evening, that’s my cue to slow it down.” That can mean cozying up with a book, brewing a cup of hot tea, or, in her case, lighting a candle at her bedside and journaling. When Salazar is finished putting her thoughts to paper, she uses the Hubspace app to adjust the color, temperature, and brightness of her lights, dimming them as she gets closer to sleep. This can even be programmed automatically in order to reduce screen time before bed.

    “Colder rooms bring better sleep, so I also have Hubspace turn on my AC at night,” she says.

    Industry observers note that the Hubspace app is free to download and easily syncs with your home’s smart devices. You can enable voice control for screen-free commands—also a plus if you’re trying to reduce your pre-sleep screen time. And the app runs on both WiFi and Bluetooth—so even if the WiFi is down, your nighttime routine can still run seamlessly.

    Movado’s New Tempo-Matic Watch Is Inspired by an Iconic Piece from the ’70s

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (276 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Movado was founded in 1881 in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, which isn’t a particularly odd backstory for a heritage Swiss watch brand.
    • Right now, a growing band of horological nerds is finding rich pickings in the Movado back catalog and pushing up vintage prices considerably—especially for its mid-century chronographs and its legendary Museum Watch (which celebrates 80 years in 2027; more of that to come) in the process.
    • Sources indicate that it’s not only the collectors who are digging into Movado’s past, however.

    Movado was founded in 1881 in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, which isn’t a particularly odd backstory for a heritage Swiss watch brand. But it has been American owned since 1983 and has a distinct quality tied deeply to its long history in the U.S. market—which puts it slightly outside the predictable purview of many watch collectors.

    Right now, a growing band of horological nerds is finding rich pickings in the Movado back catalog and pushing up vintage prices considerably—especially for its mid-century chronographs and its legendary Museum Watch (which celebrates 80 years in 2027; more of that to come) in the process.

    Sources indicate that it’s not only the collectors who are digging into Movado’s past, however. Last month, the brand released the Heritage Tempo-Matic ($995–$1,095), a re-creation of a watch that merges sporty and retro design in a neat and slinky package. The Tempo-Matic, Movado’s first automatic movement, was launched in 1945 and went on to power a broad range of Movado’s wristwatches. But the rounded yet boxy “TV” shape of the new Heritage Tempo-Matic is unmistakably 1970s, when watch design took a giant leap forward into sexy new territory.

    The 2026 version is available in three executions, each powered by the reliable Sellita SW200-1B movement and fitted with integrated steel bracelets that positively scream seventies. Two of them come in brushed steel with vertically brushed burgundy or blue dials. A third—which, we must admit, is our favorite—is gold-tone PVD with a warm gray dial. You’d be hard-pressed to find such an elegant, authentic, and affordable homage to the 1970s—a decade that’s right now a very hot motif in watch-collecting circles—anywhere else.

    How Tiffany & Co. Made a Bird on a Rock Box

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (278 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Singing Bird on a Clock and Bird on a Rock brooch, 800-843-3269.
    • Sources indicate that how does a yellow cockatoo flitting near an open window in Guadeloupe end up a jewelry icon?
    • Sources indicate that that was 1965.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Above: Tiffany & Co. Singing Bird on a Clock and Bird on a Rock brooch, 800-843-3269.

    Sources indicate that how does a yellow cockatoo flitting near an open window in Guadeloupe end up a jewelry icon? That bird knew what it was doing when it perched outside the home of Jean Schlumberger, one of Tiffany & Co’s best-known jewelry designers. Nature was always the apple of Schlumberger’s eye, and in his vision that bird would become a diamond-studded feathered friend nestled in lapis lazuli and pinned on Bunny Mellon’s beret (he would go on to make for her a full, whimsical bestiary. Theirs was a partnership of hundreds of jelly fish, camels, and seahorses, plus the beloved fruit and flowers inspired by Mellon’s own garden).

    Sources indicate that that was 1965. How to keep reaching upcoming heights? A partnership between Tiffany & Co. and the Musée des Arts Décoratifs (MAD) in Paris offers inspiration: An archive of thousands of Schlumberger’s sketches, now being restored and digitized, reveal a mind constantly at work and a vision without boundaries. And so it continues, in spessartine and chrysoprase, in rubellites and mother-of-pearl, and turquoise. The next reincarnation of the bird, though, might be one of the most exciting horological spectacles of the year: a glimmering, singing automata atop a burst of sun, a singing gold and titanium bird on a clock. Though, we must note, it does not play music: instead, it tweets. Look, and listen.

    This story originally appeared in the November 2026 matter of ELLE Decor.

    Editor-in-Chief Stellene Volandes is a jewelry expert, and the author of Jeweler: Masters and Mavericks of Modern Design (Rizzoli).

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that I am not the first person to point out that MacBooks are expensive.
    • Recent findings suggest that but the Neo is still cheap.
    • It has been revealed that designed as Apple’s answer to the lower-budget laptops running Windows, the Neo’s target audience is technically students—hence the good branding and cool colors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that I am not the first person to point out that MacBooks are expensive. I will not be the last. If you monitor this stuff like we do, you’ll have seen the irony that Apple released the budget-conscious MacBook Neo earlier this year—only for the global computing shortage to almost immediately raise the price from $599 to $699.

    Recent findings suggest that but the Neo is still cheap. You could buy it for full price and get your money’s worth—although scoring it on sale makes the whole thing even sweeter. Just in time for Black Friday, Amazon shaved $50 off of the buzzy MacBook. Chalk it up to a Christmas miracle.

    It has been revealed that designed as Apple’s answer to the lower-budget laptops running Windows, the Neo’s target audience is technically students—hence the good branding and cool colors. That being said, if you need a personal computer for watching Netflix and doing your taxes but don’t want a full desktop, it’s a perfect choice.

    The Neo runs on Apple’s A18 Pro chip—the same one that powers the iPhone 16 Pro and Pro Max. If the idea of buying a laptop that runs on a phone chip gives you pause, your stress is better channeled elsewhere. While this isn’t the right device for someone who is planning to run heavy-duty software, it can handle standard Internet browsing, video calls, and the like with ease. Just keep in mind that it has only 8 GB of RAM, so it’s best suited to basic workflows.

    It has been revealed that of course, this computer has the added benefit of four jazzy color options: blush and citrus for the bold, indigo for those more subdued, and silver for that classic MacBook aesthetic. Wrapped in an aluminum body with a 13-inch Liquid Retina display, the Neo weighs in at just 2.7 pounds (same as the MacBook Air) and is 0.5 inches thick. (For reference, the iPhone 17 Pro Max is 0.35 inches thick.).

    According to recent reports, despite our best efforts, we don’t quite know how Apple determines its deals for massive sale events, so there’s no telling if this $50 discount is as good as it’s going to get for Black Friday. In all honesty, we were hoping Amazon would shave $100 off to get the Neo back to its pre-increase price. In our wildest dreams, we’re gunning for a deal that would make this the first-ever sub-$500 MacBook.

    In a recent development, we’re not giving up on a deeper discount once Black Friday proper arrives, but for now the Neo is undoubtedly a smart buy for anyone who wants a laptop that can handle all of the basics. At $649, it’s still a fraction of the cost of the MacBook Air and Pro.

    #77703. The Rise of the Maximum Visibility Bra

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1001 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Harpersbazaar ↗ Open Full Page

    The Rise of the Maximum Visibility Bra

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The summer of 2014, I was a college student working at a small-town lingerie store that lined its walls exclusively with neutrals.
    • It has been revealed that the early 2010s set a nearly impossible goal for young women: naturally perky breasts without any apparent scaffolding.
    • Somewhere between the “free the nipple” movement in 2012 and the impending #MeToo revolution of 2017, boobs became less of a sexualized spectacle and more of a political battleground.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The summer of 2014, I was a college student working at a small-town lingerie store that lined its walls exclusively with neutrals. Every day, I sold women flesh-toned bras—black if they were really feeling kinky—all while filling my own intimates drawer with the same styles. Undressing in front of a guy that same summer, he voiced genuine disbelief over my nude, industrial-strength strapless bra. He wasn’t so much confused over its gravity-defying function as the fact that it was there, at all.

    It has been revealed that the early 2010s set a nearly impossible goal for young women: naturally perky breasts without any apparent scaffolding. But that’s all changing. Pop princess Adela’s exposed bras have become as central to her identity as her electric pink hair. Once left to jiggle freely beneath semisheer cotton, Charli XCX’s chest is now more often displayed in intricate lingerie. Several months back, Saint Laurent’s Spring 2027 front row was littered with boudoir-inspired looks while Prada and Fendi literally sent bras-as-tops down the runway. Bras have come out of hiding.

    Somewhere between the “free the nipple” movement in 2012 and the impending #MeToo revolution of 2017, boobs became less of a sexualized spectacle and more of a political battleground. Victoria’s Secret canceled its fashion show as basics-driven intimates brands like Cuup and Arq gained traction for destigmatizing natural shapes. Then, breasts bounced back into cultural focus. The shift might be credited to the climate—conservatism generally propels women to take shelter in traditional femininity, or it is thrust upon them—as well as the twin forces of Sydney Sweeney and semaglutide weight loss. Either way, women got thinner while their chests grew larger—reflecting a beauty standard we hadn’t seen in a generation. Implants entered a upcoming era of demand and dialogue, as celebrities like Kylie Jenner and Megan Fox transparently joined the major-breasted brigade.

    Industry observers note that but boobs aren’t just bigger—they’re bolder. Gone are the days of basics and bralettes. It’s all about va-va-voom underwire, satin, and lace—even push-ups have returned to the conversation. Still, “there’s a difference between showing your bra and showing off your bra,” discerns Tara Ocello, director of brand marketing at intimates brand Skarlett Blue.

    Last month, the recently revived Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show broadcast Jenner strutting down the runway, her 445-cc-moderate-profile silicones outfitted in a record-breaking $50 million bra. Bella Hadid, Candice Swanepoel, and Adriana Lima showed off the iconic mall brand’s finest embroidered balconettes, lacy push-ups, and satin plunge bras. Angels aside, the reintroduction of these runway collections is also indicative of a shift in consumer product demand—a spokesperson for Victoria’s Secret claims there’s “strong interest” in fashion-forward details like lace, satin, logo hardware, and the brand’s statement shine straps. The Very Sexy Push-Up Bra remains the number one of the three mainline bras in its “Very Sexy” category. “Today’s customer wants a bra that performs beautifully and deserves to be seen,” says a Victoria’s Secret spokesperson. “It’s expanded how customers engage with [our bras] as both foundation pieces and intentional styling elements.”.

    The luxury London retailer Agent Provocateur has been positioning its designs as statement pieces since it rolled out in the mid-’90s—the last time exposed bras enjoyed prevalence. Creative director Sarah Shotton noticed the trend bubbling several years back on the Glastonbury grounds and immediately returned to the design studio. “We predicted this and designed [for it] about a year and a half in advance. I am constantly thinking, could it be worn as an outerwear bra?” she claims. “I think if customers are going to invest in it, they want it to work harder than just in the bedroom. Lingerie as outerwear is just getting bigger and bigger.”.

    Category transcension is, of course, good for business. Victoria’s Secret reported sales up 10 percent in its second quarter, and Agent Provocateur has also seen revenue growth this year. Eager to capitalize on the movement, contemporary brands like Lioness are now engineering built-in underwear to imitate the effect of an exposed bra. This week, Charlize Theron wore a similar style by Tom Ford to the Governors Awards.

    I have, undoubtedly, been influenced. This year, I have spent more money at Victoria’s Secret than cumulatively on lingerie in the past decade—acquiring my own Very Sexy Push-Up, and a turquoise polka-dot number. These are bras I’ve never gravitated toward, let alone purchased, because they seemed like impractical additions to my wardrobe. I’ve had to ask myself: Can you wear leopard-print under a white tee? What if the lace breaches my neckline?

    Somewhere between Erin Brockovich and Blake Lively’s character in The Town, an exposed bra—particularly a colorful one—became a media shorthand for unsophistication, and more often than not, sexual availability. In simpler terms: tacky. Now, tacky is trending. Along with diamanté-encrusted snapbacks and sky-high peep-toes, straps in dynamic hues are stretched across the décolleté of It girls en masse. Printed cups are peeking out of the necklines. Some fashionistas are forgoing the shirt altogether. “There's a real cultural shift from polished perfection toward something more expressive, unpredictable, and a little undone,” claims Ocello. Or, perhaps a little more human.

    According to recent reports, this certainly isn’t a trend for everyone. According to Shotton, Agent Provocateur’s biggest sellers are corsets—a style that was once also considered strictly lingerie, but has since sashayed into the light. One wonders if their popularity is a gateway to full bra-baring, especially as GLP drugs become more readily available, and women more comfortable in their bodies. But with a Blue Wave washing in Woke 3.0, how long do boobs—and their bold accessories—have left? In all seriousness, might we look back on this moment with the same disdain we once reflected on early-aughts raunch culture? Only social media will tell. In the meantime, I plan for my collection to keep growing.

    Industry News: Who Is Daddy Franklin From ‘The Body’? For Starters, Nnamdi Asomugha Is Kerry Washington’s Husband

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you watched The Body in one sitting and are now fully obsessed with it, you’re not alone!!
    • In a recent development, though things got off to a rocky start (Kerry apparently told Nnamdi she didn’t date athletes, and Nnamdi told Kerry he didn’t date actors), the two got together anyway, and just about three years later in June 2013, they tied the knot in a super low-key ceremony.
    • Here’s everything you should know about the man behind Daddy Franklin, including how he rose to fame as a former NFL cornerback and what he’s up to next.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you watched The Body in one sitting and are now fully obsessed with it, you’re not alone!! The horrifying coming-of-age series is scary good, and while you may not be familiar with the actor who plays Father Samuel Franklin (aka Daddy Franklin), you definitely know his very famous wife. As it turns out, Nnamdi Asomugha has been married to Kerry Washington for over 13 years now, having fallen in love after watching Kerry perform in Race on Broadway in 2010. Kerry later confirmed the story during a 2018 interview with Marie Claire, saying, “The last time I did theater, it completely transformed my life. That’s where I met my husband.” Cute!!!

    In a recent development, though things got off to a rocky start (Kerry apparently told Nnamdi she didn’t date athletes, and Nnamdi told Kerry he didn’t date actors), the two got together anyway, and just about three years later in June 2013, they tied the knot in a super low-key ceremony. According to their marriage license, Kerry and Nnamdi noted “I do” in Hailey, Idaho, where Nnamdi’s sister officiated and Kerry’s parents served as witnesses. Since then, the couple has welcomed two kids together—Isabelle Amarachi, born in 2014, and Caleb Kelechi, born in 2016—and are seemingly thriving outside of the spotlight. But we think it’s time to learn a lil bit more about Nnamdi, don’t you?

    Here’s everything you should know about the man behind Daddy Franklin, including how he rose to fame as a former NFL cornerback and what he’s up to next.

    After growing up in Louisiana in a Nigerian Igbo household, Nnamdi attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he played for the California Golden Bears football team. Soon after graduating, Nnamdi was drafted in the first round of the 2003 NFL Draft by the Oakland Raiders, which is very impressive.

    It has been revealed that over his 11-year professional football career, Nnamdi also played for the Philadelphia Eagles and the San Francisco 49ers, and in December 2013, the cornerback signed a one-day contract with Oakland so he could retire as a Raider. I love to see a loyal man!

    According to Nnamdi, the decision to retire at 32 was difficult, but it still felt like the right time for him. “Yeah, I felt that it was a good time, but it didn’t make it any easier,” he told UPROXX. “It’s a game that 'til this day I miss, and I miss playing. It’s not that I want to go play again, but I miss so many aspects of it; being around the team, being around the coaching, that calm before the storm.”.

    In a recent development, nnamdi first caught the acting bug all the way back in 2008, when he landed the role of “Party Guest with Wife” on the CW sitcom The Game. (Remember: There are no small roles, only small actors!!) He then caught the eye of director Peter Berg on the set of a Nike commercial shoot in 2009, who was impressed by the athlete’s ease in front of the camera. From there, Nnamdi went on to play small roles in Friday Night Lights, Leverage, and Cubed before making his on-screen feature film debut in 2012’s Fire with Fire.

    Since retiring from the NFL, Nnamdi has fully committed himself to his acting career with starring roles in the films Crown Heights, Sylvie’s Love, The Good Nurse, The Knife, and—most recently—The Body. He’s also served as a producer on several of those projects as well.

    Despite all his success, Nnamdi still remains as modest as ever, avoiding social media and press to instead focus on his craft. “I’m really bad at self-promotion. I know that about myself,” he previously explained to Bleacher Report back in 2017. “People told me all of the time, ‘You could be such a big star if you just talked about yourself more,’ but I’m not good at that. It’s always been about team.”.

    According to recent reports, during a 2018 interview with Today, Kerry corrected a host when they alluded to her two children, saying, “I’m a mother of three." The reason: Nnamdi has a now-teenage daughter from another relationship, who Kerry has helped raise alongside her two biological children. And just like with Isabelle and Caleb, the couple keeps their eldest far from the paparazzi, so very little is known about her.

    As Kerry joked to People, “I have moments where I take pictures or videos of one of my three amazing kids and I wanna post it online, and I tend to just send it to my parents or my shrink instead.”.

    Philanthropy is crucial to Nnamdi, which is why he created the Asomugha Foundation in 2005 at the very beginning of his career.

    The foundation has two main programs: Orphans and Widows in Need (which provides food, shelter, medicine, vocational training, literacy efforts, and scholarships to widows and orphans in Nigeria) and Asomugha College Tour for Scholars (which takes selected students from Bay Area and Los Angeles area high schools on college tours across the country).

    It has been revealed that though Kerry and Nnamdi are both actors and producers, it isn’t often that they work together on creative projects. Back in 2017, Nnamdi told Vanity Fair that it was possible he and his wife would co-produce a project at some point.

    “We would produce,” he mentioned. “We’d probably produce before acting, I would think.” The following year, his production company, iAm21 Entertainment, helped produce American Son, a Broadway play starring Kerry, and hopefully, that won’t be the last time the two are involved in the same project.

    As far as sharing the screen goes, however, Nnamdi doesn’t think that will ever happen. As he told The New York Times, “I produced American Son, but as actors, there’s no proposal as of now for that collaboration. We’re very supportive of each other’s journeys, but we’ve always been that way. We always want the best for each other in whatever we’re doing.”.

    Case in point? The couple’s *chef’s kiss* appearance at the 2025 Met Gala. Ahem:.

    Oh, and the duo’s 2025 Golden Globes looks:.

    Sources indicate that and ofc, he was right by Kerry's side during her December 2024 Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony, where she finally received her well-deserved star. How cute do they look with Kerry's parents??

    Sources indicate that TL;DR: Kerry and Nnamdi truly couldn’t be any cuter. Keep on being adorably low-key, you two.

    As one of the leaders of modern-day minimalism, it makes sense that Hailey Bieber would wink to the woman who arguably started it all: Carolyn Bessette Kennedy.

    This afternoon, Mrs. Bieber attended the 2026 DealBook Summit in Lincoln Center—a conference that unites some of the biggest leaders in tech, business, and politics—to discuss her mega-successful beauty brand, Rhode.

    At the summit, she pulled out a supreme fashion reference, with an archival set from the Yohji Yamamoto Spring/Summer 1998 collection, once worn by none other than serious Yamamoto enthusiast CBK.

    The finely tailored look consisted of a black Mandarin-collar jacket with a pinched waist and a split hem, plus a row of matching buttons dotting the front.

    It was paired with a cream linen midi skirt that hugged Bieber’s legs, and for accessories, she matched the jacket with inky patent-leather pumps and one of CBK’s favorite finishing touches: an acetate headband.

    Bessette Kennedy famously wore this look back in June 1998, when she attended the Robin Hood Foundation benefit with her husband, John F. Kennedy Jr., at the 26th Street Armory in Upcoming York City. For the occasion, she tied her hair back into a ponytail and went sans jewelry.

    We were all reminded of CBK’s chic style earlier this year, when FX released the smash Love Story: John F. Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette miniseries. Stars like Bella Hadid and Sarah Pidgeon (the latter of whom portrayed Bessette Kennedy in the show) all seemed to take a page out of the former Calvin Klein publicist’s styling book for their own outfits. And Bieber also joined in on the fun.

    Sources indicate that but while many have tried to recreate the late muse’s look, few can really capture the true essence of CBK. Clearly, Bieber is one of them.

    Tech Report: Why Men Are Posting Thirst Traps in Red Light Face Masks

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, gonzalo Fernández Escribano knew all about the benefits of red-light therapy for his skin.
    • Recent findings suggest that "I use my red-light mask right before bed, so I’m already shirtless,” says Escribano.
    • Escribano is one of many men online who’ve embraced the red-light thirst trap.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, gonzalo Fernández Escribano knew all about the benefits of red-light therapy for his skin. Fewer wrinkles, a brighter complexion, minimizing acne—he’d experienced it all firsthand when he tried out LED masks during his facials. In March 2025, he purchased one for at-home use. Little did he know it would come with an extra benefit as a provocative prop for a sexy photo.

    Recent findings suggest that "I use my red-light mask right before bed, so I’m already shirtless,” says Escribano. “Let’s just say the sexy-looking picture is easily convenient to take.”.

    Escribano is one of many men online who’ve embraced the red-light thirst trap. More and more, image-conscious guys with followings built around some combination of beauty, fitness, wellness, travel, are pairing their red-light routines with the occasional shirtless selfie. The trend is especially prevalent in gay-male internet culture, where faceless torsos shots, sometimes featuring beefy chests and six-pack abs, have been part of the visual language of dating apps and social media for years. A shirtless red-light-mask pic is a variation on the theme: The body and the anonymity are still there—only now there’s a skincare routine attached.

    It has been revealed that jayson Stacy, a celebrity groomer, noticed his friend wearing an LED in his Instagram profile picture three years ago. At the same time, Stacy had recently gotten a mask himself and decided to follow suit, posting a photo of his own after Mardi Gras under the guise of some much needed recovery.

    “It’s almost like a sexy Halloween costume, but you don’t have to wait until October,” Stacy says. Escribano agrees, saying it makes him look like a superhero. Strong shadows, glowing skin, and a Sith-like red glow mix together in a thirsty trifecta meant to slow someone’s scrolling.

    Industry observers note that for Stacy, red-light masks strike the perfect balance between wellness and plausible deniability. “You’re supposed to use the mask after you wash your face, so most are fresh out of the shower before using,” he notes. “It’s like, ‘Oh, look at my morning routine,’ which gives the perfect excuse to be mostly unclothed. Then you have the mask on, you feel like someone can’t see your face, so it can feel like a layer of protection.” In other words, the skin care routine becomes the reason for the thirst trap, even though it’s only half the motivation.

    Red-light therapy is a noninvasive treatment that uses low-level LED light to stimulate cellular activity and boost collagen production. The technology has become especially prominent over the last few years thanks to its ability to reduce inflammation, soften fine lines, and promote skin and muscle recovery and hair growth. (That is, as long as you are willing to invest in high-quality equipment and use it every single day).

    Celebrities have been documenting their LED routines for years, from January Jones to Kim Kardashian. But those posts were mostly framed around the masks’ intended purpose: improving your skin. Somewhere along the way, though, a certain breed of extremely online men—trainers, models, artists, content creators, and guys who simply know their angles—found a second purpose for the masks: as an accessory for a hot photo. The masks are turning up in bathroom mirror pics, bedroom shots, and buried several slides deep in otherwise unrelated photo dumps, often without any mention of skin care at all. And judging by the comments—fire emojis, heart eyes, and the occasional “yummy”—their followers seem to be noticing something other than the mask.

    Recent findings suggest that the thirst traps are also surfacing on social media at a time when curiosity around red-light therapy is booming. A 2025 study analyzing Google Trends data found that search interest across red-light-therapy-related terms increased 118% after February 2024. And by 2025, Google reported that searches for “red light therapy” had reached an all-time high. As these futuristic devices have rapidly flooded our feeds, maybe it was only a matter of time before they made their way out of the skin care selfie and into something a little thirstier.

    Recent findings suggest that in some ways these images are being ushered into well-trodden territory. In 2021, TikTok’s viral Silhouette Challenge had customers transform themselves into barely distinguishable, body-forward silhouettes under a red filter, turning the color itself into a visual shorthand for sex appeal. Meanwhile, for gay men, shirtless photos are hardly a novelty, especially on dating apps like Grindr and Sniffies, where headless torsos are practically part of the experience. “The headless torsos definitely all blend together at this point,” notes John Arthur Hill, who compares swiping through hookup apps to looking into “a lukewarm batch of Chili’s skillet queso” and trying to figure out what’s cheese, meat, or a bell pepper.

    And even when the most impressive six-pack can get lost in an endless doom scroll, red light can add just enough intrigue to get someone to look twice. For Adam Pent, an OnlyFans creator who’s no stranger to posting thirst traps himself, that curiosity is part of the appeal. “It [a red-light-mask thirst trap] is definitely more interesting because I’d be curious about who’s behind the mask,” he says. To Pent, there’s something creative about the whole thing. “I guess it makes the photo a bit more artful too? ‘Art thot’ vibes I guess, unless it looks like sponsored content.” It also makes him want to shop. “I’m less focused on the body and more like, ‘Should I just get one already?’”.

    According to recent reports, the red-light thirst trap also holds a certain mysterious appeal. “I’ve been posting ‘masked’ selfies for quite some time because I think it’s a really hot aesthetic and such a cool fantasy,” Michael Anthony, a celebrity makeup artist, says. For him, it’s not just about looking good in the photos. “The fantasy of anonymity and pleasure, while doing something for yourself that will make you look and feel better—it’s all so sexy.”.

    An LED face mask is a luxurious way to get an at-home glow, and Shark's is one of our favorites. It helps to fight acne and fine lines, and it can help depuff around the eyes for those long nights.

    It has been revealed that tattoo artist Alvin Archibald sees a similar appeal. “There’s a subtle tension between vulnerability and control that makes it interesting,” he indicates. “The mask takes away your facial expressions, so the body becomes the focus. It creates this interesting dynamic where you’re both exposed and concealed at the same time. There’s something almost intimate about it, like you’re getting ready for an audience without necessarily admitting it.”.

    According to recent reports, if it feels like life is one long string of sales—most of them being mediocre—you’re not wrong. Despite the near-constant deluge of Prime Days, anniversary events, and the like, some sales do legitimately stand above the rest. You know the one: Black Friday. It tends to bring some of the best deals of the year, including record-low prices on Apple tech.

    Apple is notorious for not marking down its own products—on the contrary, the tech giant actually raised prices on Macs and iPads earlier this year—so we turn to retailers like Amazon when looking to save on everything from AirPods to Apple Watches. This year, Amazon’s Black Friday deals span 12 days (the sale is called Turkey 12 if you’d like to know too much), which means plenty of Apple discounts are already live. In the event that you’ve spilled coffee on your MacBook or lost one of your AirPods, you needn’t wait until Black Friday proper to shop.

    It has been revealed that sure, there’s always the chance these deals could slightly deepen, but we’d wager we’re only looking at marginal price cuts at this point. Consider this: Shop now, shave a couple hundred bucks off of those tech upgrades you’ve been avoiding, then spend your holiday weekend watching football and reheating Thanksgiving leftovers instead of scrolling through Amazon. Your move.

    Industry observers note that airPods reliably go on deep discount during Amazon sale events, and Black Friday has proven no different. The third-generation AirPods Pro have dropped to just $179, only $10 shy of their record-low price.

    Sources indicate that although the fresh AirPods 5 aren’t marked down right now, they start at just $129, which is still lower than the discounted Pros. We’re hoping that these will go on sale for the first time on Black Friday. For those who prefer over-ear headphones, the AirPods Max 2 are $120 off (not quite their lowest price, but nothing to scoff at). You can also save on Beats wireless headphones and earbuds, including $150 off the ultra-popular Beats Studio Pro, which have Apple’s chip under the hood.

    No Apple product experienced higher price hikes than laptops. The MacBook Air jumped $200 to $1,299 and the MacBook Pro climbed $400 to $1,999, driven by rising RAM and storage costs. To ease the pain, both the 13- and 15-inch MacBook Air models are up to 19% off. We haven’t seen deals this deep on Macs in quite some time.

    If you prefer the Pro, those aren’t quite as discounted, but you can still shave up to $250 off of a souped-up model. Plus, Apple’s most affordable laptop, the MacBook Neo, just went on sale for the first time. Sure, it’s only a $50 discount, but it’s still the cheapest model by far—and fits the bill for most basic needs like watching Netflix and renewing your lease.

    Apple MacBook Pro 16-Inch (M5 Pro).

    Apple MacBook Neo 13-inch (A18 Pro).

    Although Apple Watches haven’t fallen victim to price increases this year, deals have been few and far between, which means these Black Friday discounts are liable to sell out fast.

    Sources indicate that the brand-new Apple Watch Series 12—which ushered in Apple’s first stab at readiness scores—is $70 off, dropping this to its lowest price ever. If you’re looking for a budget-friendly Apple Watch, opt for the SE 3, which has dipped to under $200—a verifiable steal given Apple’s current pricing dynamics. While the rugged Apple Watch Ultra 4 isn’t on sale right now, we’ll keep you posted should any surprise sales arise.

    Apple Watch Series 12 (GPS, 42mm).

    Apple Watch Series 12 (GPS+ Cellular, 42mm).

    Industry observers note that back in June, Apple bumped the price of its entire iPad range by up to $200, which makes scoring one on sale all the more crucial. As predicted, previous-gen iPad Minis (an editor favorite) are $100 off after the revamped A20 Pro model was released earlier this month. Should you prefer a full-sized tablet, entry-level iPads, iPad Airs, and iPad Pros are all on sale, so it’s mostly a matter of use case in determining which to buy. If you’re going to watch TV on it while traveling, opt for the $399 model, while the Pro is better suited for getting creative work done.

    Sources indicate that accessories are reliably among the easiest Apple products to save on during major sales. If you want to stick with Apple-branded gear, the second-generation AirTag, complete with improved Precision Finding, is sitting at a record-low $23, in addition to discounts on Apple Pencils, Magic Keyboards, and the like. You can also save on plenty of third-party power banks, wall adapters, and wireless chargers, which tend to see steeper discounts than Apple’s own gear.

    Apple AirTag (2nd Generation) - 4 Pack.

    Industry News: APC Just Dropped a Pair of Incredibly Clean Casios

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (442 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Gq

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that we’re in a great era for affordable fashion-collab watches.
    • Industry observers note that the first collaboration between the two brands saw them rework the hallowed A1000 digital-display watch.
    • That part is the opposite of loud: as with the previous collab, there isn’t much giving away the brand's participation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that we’re in a great era for affordable fashion-collab watches. Timex is leading the way: its link-ups with Noah, Todd Snyder, and J. Crew are masterclasses in adding personality to classic designs without going OTT. But don’t count Casio out of the race. The Japanese giant has just followed up its 2024 collab with APC. The pair are perfectly matched: Casio watches are known for being beautifully functional and understated—adjectives that fit APC’s spartan aesthetic too.

    Industry observers note that the first collaboration between the two brands saw them rework the hallowed A1000 digital-display watch. That release stripped back a lot of the original’s markings and added the APC logo on the dial. This time around, it's the AQ-240 getting a makeover. The case is squarer than the rectangular A1000, and while there’s a narrow window for a digital display, the watch maintains the traditional analog format with hands and hour markers. Here, you get the best of both worlds. The watch is sold out on APC's website but still available through Casio, so act fast if you want one. The silver variant is $110, and the gold goes for $135.

    What about the APC-ness of it all? That part is the opposite of loud: as with the previous collab, there isn’t much giving away the brand's participation. We’ve got the APC logo on the dial and the buckle, plus the brand’s guitar-and-dagger insignia engraved out of sight on the caseback. Casio already offers the regular A1000 in a bunch of different colorways, but these two upcoming ones are made specifically for the APC collab. The release includes a silver case with a dark-green dial and another in gold on gold. Both of the pieces have a brushed sun-ray effect on the dial. The vibe is refined and stripped back; this is a fashion watch that almost feels anti-fashion.

    Maybe the best way to think about it is as the reverse side of the coin to the excellent new G-Shock 2500 Series. Both come from Casio, and both are minimal and functional. But the G-Shocks are big and bulky, with a design that seems to tip its hat to Patek Philippe’s Nautilus. These new ones are slim and nearly dressy. Put the two new releases together, and you’ve got pretty much all bases covered. And if those aforementioned Timex collabs felt a bit too classicist for you, then the Casio-APC partnership takes things in a more modern direction. Far from just being a cash grab, the “fashion watch” is now one of the best routes into affordable, on-point horology.

    This story originally appeared on British GQ.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, one of the most legendary entertainers in American history, Liberace dazzled audiences for decades with his over-the-top piano medleys, flamboyant costumes, and cheeky banter. The self-described “Mr. Showmanship” might be synonymous with Las Vegas, where he had a popular residency, but he also had a taste for Palm Springs, owning no fewer than four homes in the California desert oasis throughout his life.

    In a recent development, now, perhaps the most exceptional of those properties, a 1930s Spanish Revival estate—dubbed the Cloisters due to its network of arcades and courtyards—has hit the market for $6.9 million. Elsewhere in Southern California, the longtime Beverly Hills home of Hollywood power couple Annette Bening and Warren Beatty is also newly for sale, asking almost $15 million. And on the East Coast, Lady Gaga’s former penthouse atop Manhattan’s Hit Factory building is available for $7 million, while the most expensive home in Charleston just listed for $35 million. Check them all out below.

    In a recent development, acquired at the height of his career in the late 1960s, Liberace’s walled Spanish Colonial Revival estate in Palm Springs just hit the market for nearly $6.9 million. The famed entertainer turned the 1930s bed-and-breakfast, known as the Cloisters, into an extension of his opulent stage set, brimming with signature candelabras, opulent furnishings, and splashes of gold. He lived on the half-acre property until his death in 1987, after which fresh owners have completely remodeled the 8,000-square-foot home to bring it back to its original splendor. HGTV host Brett Waterman spearheaded the most recent patch, filling the five-bedroom home with handcrafted details and understated furnishings. Perks include a heated in-ground pool, courtyards, and a spa facing the San Jacinto Mountains. It’s listed with Keith Markovitz and Rick Distel of TTK Represents at Compass.

    On Wednesday, ELLE Decor exclusively reported that the longtime Beverly Hills home of Warren Beatty and Annette Bening was hitting the market for the first time since they sold it. The Hollywood power couple custom-built the gated residence in 1992 and raised their four kids there, selling it in 2012 to hotelier Jonathan Baker and his wife, Jenny. They spearheaded their own revamp to the tune of $5 million, bringing a contemporary spirit to the interiors of the nine-bedroom compound, which includes a guest house, pool, and tennis court. Its new asking price is $14.995 million.

    According to recent reports, last year, a 225-year-old mansion smashed the record for the most expensive home sold in Charleston, fetching a little over $21 million. Now, another estate is vying for the title. The Sword Gate House, located in the South Carolina city’s historic South of Broad neighborhood, just listed for $35 million with Leslie Turner of Maison Real Estate. Revamped by interior designer Cortney Bishop, the 17,140-square-foot mansion dates to the early 1800s and features preserved millwork, exposed brick, and an original mural in the dining room depicting historic Charleston harbor. There are also uncommon perks like a triple-decker piazza, a ballroom, a pool, and an acre of manicured gardens. The whole compound is secured behind preserved wrought-iron gates made by local ironworker Christopher Werner, giving the landmark its moniker.

    According to recent reports, forget a “Million Reasons”—we’re looking at $7 million. The New York City penthouse where Lady Gaga once lived just hit the market for nearly $7 million—and she’s not the home’s only celebrity connection. The 3,700-square-foot duplex was also once home to former NBA star Carmelo Anthony and 30 Rock actor Tracy Morgan, per People.

    It has been revealed that with its organic silhouette, cantilevered roofline, and clever use of space, Leuthold House by Allan Gelbin bears the hallmarks of his mentor, legendary architect Frank Lloyd Wright. Completed in 1966 on five rolling acres in New Canaan, the five-bedroom house spans roughly 5,700 square feet and underwent a restoration by Hobbs Inc. and JMK Architects in 2014. The interiors feature long expanses of glass and mahogany, while the grounds come with a spring-fed pond, a pool, a one-bedroom guest house, and 150 specimen trees. Listed for $6.2 million with John Engel and Melissa Engel of Douglas Elliman, the two-story house is on the market for the first time in 29 years.

    Recent findings suggest that geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

    This St. Bart’s House Was Designed to Look Nothing Like Its Neighbors

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1076 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, few clients ask their designer to make the bedrooms in their vacation home smaller and simpler, but that was just the edit the homeowners made to plans for their house in St.
    • In a recent development, situated on a steep hillside above one of St.
    • In a recent development, A Caribbean island is a challenging place to work under any circumstances.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, few clients ask their designer to make the bedrooms in their vacation home smaller and simpler, but that was just the edit the homeowners made to plans for their house in St. Bart’s, states designer David Ries. “They didn’t want these humongous bedrooms with huge floating beds and massive bathrooms.” Instead, the couple wanted to be able to host as many people as possible, a request that didn’t surprise Ries, who’d already worked with the family on homes in Manhattan, Long Island, and Telluride. “It’s what this client has always asked for. They can’t have enough bedrooms.”.

    In a recent development, situated on a steep hillside above one of St. Bart’s famously pristine white sand beaches, the house had initially been a boutique hotel. The plan was to turn it into a retreat for themselves and their adult children and grandchildren. The family are longtime visitors to the island—“the daughter told me it was her ‘happy place,’” claims Ries, lead designer of the Upcoming York-based interior design firm Ries Hayes—and knew exactly what they wanted. Not the white box look popular with luxury new builds on the island, but instead something reminiscent of the “old St. Bart’s,” says East Hampton-based landscape designer Edwina von Gal, who, like Ries, has collaborated with the clients on other projects.

    In a recent development, A Caribbean island is a challenging place to work under any circumstances. Everything has to be brought in from far away, including all the plants, which came by barge from Miami. St. Bart’s in particular requires anyone building to work with a local architect and engineer. In their initial proposal, this French team defaulted to that “slick and modernist” look, as von Gal describes it, with the oversized bedrooms and white color scheme that dominates much of the island’s luxury housing stock.

    Sources indicate that the design team pushed back—asking for a lot of bedrooms (eight) and generous living spaces. They also had strong opinions on the building materials. Given the island’s climate, the humid, salt-soaked air can be hard on everything. “If we did white paint, which is prominent throughout St. Bart's, it’s constant maintenance, constant painting,” says Ries. The design team insisted on cladding the buildings in Ipe, the durable tropical hardwood, which wears well. It mystified the local architects and set the complex apart from its neighbors. It also makes the buildings disappear into the greenery of the hillside.

    But the architects quickly caught on to the new plans, and von Gal is eager to praise their technical accomplishments. Regulations require properties to conserve rainwater, so there are cisterns beneath the buildings, plus technology infrastructure and laundry facilities. “Working on the hill is so complex,” she notes. “It's such a tight little package of technology and function. What they did was amazing.”.

    The team decided to reconfigure the property as a series of pavilions that face the view of the ocean and surrounding hills. The main entry is at the top of the steep hill, along with parking. The next level down is for family bedrooms; below that is a primary suite and study; and finally the fourth level is the main living space, including a playroom. “We made sure this playroom was front and center,” states Ries. “My client loves her grandkids.”.

    Sources indicate that the playroom and study have built-in daybeds that can be used as spare guest rooms in a pinch. But the clients did get their eight bedrooms. “We know how to make compact bedrooms and make them very efficient, make them very livable, which allows us to fit in a lot of space for a lot of guests, and then that puts a lot of emphasis on having main entertaining spaces that are big and gracious,” notes Ries. “The idea is that everybody hangs out together.”.

    Everything is united by generous outdoor spaces, which wind between the bedrooms. “Every room has an amazing view,” notes Ries. “It feels almost like your own little treehouse in a way.” The bottom living area opens out to a pool and an expansive deck where the family eats most of their meals.

    The house has an elevator, but stairs are the primary way the family moves between levels and finally down to the beach. “We hung on for a really great, gracious, fun set of stairs,” indicates von Gal. “They really introduce you to how amazing the different levels are and all the wonderful secret places.”.

    In a recent development, durable fabrics and materials were chosen throughout and Ries made sure everything could be easily moved around and reconfigured. Outside on the main deck, three long dining tables from Sutherland were outfitted with casters so they could be maneuvered into a single long table or several smaller ones; 26 lightweight dining chairs can be pulled from different parts of the deck. If the infamous “Christmas winds” bring a downpour, the tables can even be moved indoors so a dinner party can proceed in inclement weather. Outdoor seating can be arranged as a 15-foot sofa or several love seats.

    Industry observers note that “It's so flexible,” says Ries. “We know this from working with a client that their needs for entertaining change every day, or sometimes a couple times a day.”.

    According to recent reports, the kitchen is also efficient, designed to produce easy, clean meals. The family would rather spend time in the pool than over a stove. And no part of the living room is oriented around a TV. “They're readers,” states Ries. “There’s always stacks of new books when you go to their homes. So there’s all these cool little spots you can tuck into.”.

    It has been revealed that ultimately, the client and design team’s insistence on what they wanted paid off—but it wasn’t without a few moments of doubt. “When so many people are telling you ‘no, surely this is not what you want,’ it does start to erode your confidence a little,” notes von Gal. “Then when it does come out well, there’s a real sense of triumph and satisfaction.”.

    Tour this St. Bart’s Family Home.

She has written for The Fresh York Times and Town & Country and was most recently the Editor in Chief of Romper. She lives in Brooklyn, New York with her family.

    #77674. Are You a Super Ager? This Competition Will Be the Judge of That

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1373 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gq ↗ Open Full Page

    Are You a Super Ager? This Competition Will Be the Judge of That

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1373 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Alan Krepack stands with his hands on his hips and takes a deep breath as he sizes up the Over Under: an obstacle with a high wooden box and low wooden beam spread 10 meters apart.
    • It has been revealed that as soon as the volunteer notes “go” he sprints to the box, plants his hands, and hoists his feet up and over.
    • Industry observers note that the challenge is just the first of eight trials Krepeck will tackle throughout the day alongside his sons, Harrison and Aaron, at the Super Age Games, a fitness and mental competition designed to assess abilities associated with healthy aging.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Alan Krepack stands with his hands on his hips and takes a deep breath as he sizes up the Over Under: an obstacle with a high wooden box and low wooden beam spread 10 meters apart. Music booms over the speakers and other competitors shuffle around the cavernous room of the Armory Track in Washington Heights, Fresh York, but Krepack stays laser-focused, thanks to years of meditation practice.

    It has been revealed that as soon as the volunteer notes “go” he sprints to the box, plants his hands, and hoists his feet up and over. As he lands on the other side, he sprints to the beam, dropping down into an army crawl. “Take your time, take your time,” his son yells from the sidelines. Krepack reaches the far end, rushes back, and repeats the sequence again before crossing the line in 51 seconds. To cool down, he paces back and forth with his hands on his head. “I think I’m a sprinter, I’m a jumper, but then it’s like, fuck, no, I’m 73 years old,” he says, catching his breath.

    Industry observers note that the challenge is just the first of eight trials Krepeck will tackle throughout the day alongside his sons, Harrison and Aaron, at the Super Age Games, a fitness and mental competition designed to assess abilities associated with healthy aging. On November 7th, the inaugural day-long event drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries, and about 70% of participants were between the ages of 40 and 64. Krepeck agreed to let me shadow him to understand this newly introduced event through the lens of someone who is, in fact, aging, and would like to do so gracefully.

    The name of the Games comes from a buzzword that originated in the longevity world: super ager. The term was originally coined by Northwestern University researchers to describe adults over 80 whose memories rival those of people 30 years younger. These days it’s thrown around on podcasts and in books to describe anyone who defies both the typical trajectory of both cognitive and physical aging.

    The inaugural Super Age Games drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries.

    From crawling across a cargo net to reading microexpressions, the challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill. At the end, athletes see where they rank among their age group and receive their “Super Age,” learning how their body’s physical fitness stacks up against the general U.S. population’s.

    In a recent development, in an era where your average middle-aged midwestern dad is training for Hyrox, and a upcoming, outlandishly extreme challenge is being invented every few months, the Super Age games are a low-key counterpoint to raw, stunty, athleticism, born from the metric-obsessed fitness subcultures who prize longevity above all. And now that fitness trackers like Whoop or Apple Watch can track VO2max, heart rate variability, and resting heart rates, that group continues to grow. Along the way, these stats have become status symbols on par with owning a Lamborghini. And now that overall health is quantifiable, fitness values have become less about just how fast you run or how much you lift, but how slowly aging.

    According to recent reports, it follows that, despite its name, Super Age Games isn’t just for aging athletes. The crowd there leaned middle-aged, and the youngest person at the competition was 21. As we stood by the dead hang station, Krepak pointed across the room at a brolic young man who looked like he could be an NFL prospect: “That dude’s a serious athlete,” he says, as we watched him run around the track cradling a sandbag on his shoulder.

    Industry observers note that unlike competitions like Hyrox, where athletes race through a sequence of workouts against the clock, the Super Age Games allows competitors to rest as long as they need between trials. In fact, Junior Kennedy, the fitness program director for the Games, encourages it. “There's no rush,” he notes. “The goal is to get through each event as intentionally as you can. We need to understand what it means to recover.”.

    Each trial was developed with a certain longevity marker in mind, and developed with input from researchers at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, a leading nonprofit research center based in Novato, California dedicated to understanding aging. The Over Under, for example, tests agility by judging how fast you can change levels and switch directions. Meanwhile, the Synapse, a challenge where participants track moving balls on a screen and identify them after they've been shuffled around, is meant to measure cognitive processing.

    Challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill.

    Krepack, a psychologist and lifelong athlete from Mill Valley, California, first heard about the event through its founder, David Stewart. Stewart is a media founder behind two niche longevity platforms, AGEIST and Super Age, where he writes about longevity, wellness, and redefining aging (one of his website testimonial’s says he has made aging “cool and aspirational.”). Krepack’s generally a skeptic of the profit-driven modern wellness industry—“I've always had a jaded view of all of that stuff,” he says—but he has followed both Stewart and the Buck Institutes’ work for years.

    Sources indicate that the competition appealed to Krepack, in part because he’s spent decades cultivating a consistent exercise routine he’s proud of. He played baseball in college and has spent much of his life skiing, cycling, and playing other sports. These days, his schedule revolves around a handful of rituals: bike rides on Mondays and Fridays, a Saturday hike with a friend, gardening, yoga, and Zen meditation most days. When he signed up for the Games in June, he altered his exercise routine, lifted more weights, practiced hanging from a bar, and experimented with the Neurotracker cognitive test online.

    According to recent reports, yet all that training didn’t prepare Krepack for the biggest surprise of his day. After scoring well on both the Inferno (the assault bike VO2max test) and Synapse, next came the fourth trial: the “Tightrope,” a balance challenge that requires competitors to walk along a low beam while carrying a water-filled bag, taking as many consecutive steps as they can in two minutes without falling. He had expected to excel, thanks to years of skiing and yoga. Instead, he struggled to keep steady as the water shifted inside the bag. As his foot slipped off the bar, his eyes got wide. “I can’t believe my balance,” he says. “That’s my one disappointment in life now.”.

    Alan Krepack's sons Harrison and Aaron during the “tightrope” challenge.

    Krepack was still hard on himself as we walked over to the dead hang trial. But after beating both his sons’ times, he seemed to get his competitive spirit back. He pushed through the remaining challenge determined to finish strong. And he did: By the end of the Games, he had placed second overall, with scores adjusted for age.

    A few days after the competition, I checked in with Krepack to ask him how he’d processed the event. He responded with screenshots of his scores. His highest score came from the cargo net, which he credited to sheer determination rather than any particular finesse: “due to my will and overcoming an unconventional and desperate style!” he texted me, “Plus my sons were great support and focus partners.”.

    Sources indicate that but the Games were also a reality check about aging: “I left there feeling both young and old,” he tells me on a phone call. As he watched his sons rocket through the obstacles, he was forced to confront how much of his athleticism he’d lost. “They just flew over it. They were so fluid, and so fast,” he claims. “I’m not 30 or 40 or 50 or 60 anymore.”.

    Industry observers note that despite all the longevity industry's promises of maintaining youth, Krepack sees little value in denying the inevitable. Aging well, he claims, is about “accepting, improving, and doing your best. It’s not a denial of who you are at this point in life.” The goal, he says, is to make the most of what you’re still capable of.

    #77669. ELLE Decor Checks In: The Cooper, Charleston

    ELLE Decor Checks In: The Cooper, Charleston

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Founded as a seaport more than 350 years ago, Charleston evolved into one of the most crucial trade hubs in colonial America.
    • Located on the site of the former State Ports Authority headquarters (which was demolished in 2019), the 191-key property sits on Charleston’s historic peninsula and overlooks the Cooper River.
    • “We wanted The Cooper to feel like a natural extension of the city, balancing the ease of a waterfront home with the refinement of a luxury hotel,” says Jun Chun, principal at Champalimaud Design.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Founded as a seaport more than 350 years ago, Charleston evolved into one of the most crucial trade hubs in colonial America. As the South Carolina city’s wealth grew, handsome estates began filling up its coastline. But throughout Charleston’s rich, colorful, and complicated history, the city never had a high-end hotel that took full advantage of its waterfront setting—until this year, with the debut of The Cooper.

    Located on the site of the former State Ports Authority headquarters (which was demolished in 2019), the 191-key property sits on Charleston’s historic peninsula and overlooks the Cooper River. Interiors by Champalimaud Design pay homage to the city’s maritime heritage, referencing the “Lowcountry” culture that took root in the surrounding region.

    “We wanted The Cooper to feel like a natural extension of the city, balancing the ease of a waterfront home with the refinement of a luxury hotel,” says Jun Chun, principal at Champalimaud Design. “The overall inspiration was Charleston itself, particularly its coastal heritage, architectural history, and gracious, unhurried way of life.”.

    In a recent development, the six-story property, which is operated by Beemok Hospitality Collection, has a relaxed feel infused with a subtle Southern flavor. The experience starts before guests even step inside thanks to an entryway lined with an allée of crepe myrtle trees—a Charleston staple with tumbles of showy, hot-pink blooms.

    Inside, the lobby sports creamy marble flooring with a basketweave pattern that nods to the local art of braiding sweetgrass. Meanwhile, a mural inspired by changing tides lines the spiral staircase, leading to the public areas upstairs.

    Industry observers note that the hotel’s Mediterranean-style signature restaurant, The Crossing, helmed by chef Nick Dugan, was designed by multidisciplinary studio Meyer Davis. (There are three additional, smaller dining venues on site.) For the restaurant’s meandering floor blueprint, the design team created a series of distinct indoor and outdoor spaces, hewing to a marshland palette of soothing neutrals and calming blues as well as strategic doses of lacquer, teak, and honey onyx.

    References to the local culture continue in the guest rooms, which feature bespoke headboards, wardrobes, and credenzas adorned with woven details, once again tying back to vernacular craft. “We approached the guest rooms as elegant waterfront homes rather than traditional hotel rooms,” states Chun. “Wide-plank oak floors, painted shiplap walls, woven textures, and residential-style Roman shades establish a sense of warmth and familiarity.”.

    Among the amenities are a 7,000-square-foot spa as well as a heated saltwater infinity-edge pool on the fourth-floor terrace. The pool deck, which has its own bar, overlooks not just the harbor but even more perks: a fresh waterfront park by Rees Roberts + Partners plus a private marina, where guests can charter one of the property’s cruising vessels, such as a Hinckley motor yacht.

    It has been revealed that for the design team, bringing The Cooper to life was a careful balance of respecting tradition while also looking forward. “Charleston has an extraordinary architectural heritage and a strong tradition of craftsmanship, and we wanted to acknowledge those qualities without simply reproducing the past,” explains Chun.

    “Ultimately, we wanted The Cooper to feel as though it belongs in Charleston today and will continue to feel relevant for years to come.”.

    Geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.
